title: Readout Dependent Parameter Identifiability of Quantum Kernels
authors: Hyong Keun Park, Jahoon Jeong, Joonkyo Shim, Hyunsoo Yoon
abstract: A circuit parameter can change measured features without changing their projected Gaussian kernel. We characterize this lost dependence and distinguish recovery by metric design from nonlinear feature expansion. With analytic feature coefficients, a fixed finite data basis affinely independent on the input domain, a fixed positive definite metric, and fixed bandwidth, the coefficient Gram matrix determines all-input kernel equivalence, global coordinate inactivity, and generic differential rank. An exact four-qubit family exhibits a sharp boundary: diagonal metrics give rank two, dense metrics reach but cannot exceed three, and no fixed affine expansion crosses this ceiling. One appended nonlinear scalar coordinate suffices for rank four and is minimal when the original features are retained. A single pairwise product achieves this with an explicit nondiagonal metric; a scalar sum of two products achieves it with a diagonal metric. Both use existing ideal local means. Exact certificates establish ranks in 54 selected circuit/readout settings. Matched finite-shot comparisons show that minimal representation size need not give the best sensitivity among the tested designs. Under a factorized measurement distribution, conditional product estimation cannot increase variance at a fixed design. Execution audits further separate kernel identifiability from compiled cost.
summary: This work rigorously analyzes when quantum kernels are uniquely determined by their measurement outcomes, establishing that kernel equivalence is equivalent to the equality of coefficient Gram matrices. It quantifies the limits of parameter identifiability for small quantum systems, showing how nonlinear feature expansions can recover lost information. The findings are vital for designing robust quantum measurement protocols.
main_problem: The paper characterizes the parameter identifiability of quantum kernels, determining which physical parameter distinctions survive readout measurements and how lost dependence can be recovered.
main_result: Kernel equivalence is shown to be equivalent to the equality of the coefficient Gram matrices, and the authors establish specific rank boundaries for small quantum systems using minimal nonlinear feature expansions.
method: The analysis relies on characterizing the coefficient Gram matrix $G(	heta) = C(	heta)^T M C(	heta)$ to determine kernel equivalence and generic differential rank, comparing this to state geometry via the Quantum Fisher Information (QFI).
model_or_system: The study uses quantum kernels derived from projected Gaussian kernels based on expectation values of Pauli observables ($	ext{Tr}[ho_	heta(x) O_j]$) for quantum circuits.
key_observables: Coefficient Gram matrix $G(	heta)$, generic differential rank, kernel equivalence, and variance ratios in estimation protocols.
important_parameters: Circuit parameters ($	heta$), metric design (diagonal vs. dense), and the number of qubits (e.g., four-qubit family).
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on 'ideal-model' comparisons and assumes specific algebraic structures (e.g., finite Laurent polynomials) for decidability guarantees.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate connections between different state/feature representations yielding the same kernel, and show rank limits for the four-qubit family under various metric choices.
paper_structure: The paper develops from establishing the equivalence between kernel equality and Gram matrix equality (Theorem 1), to deriving conditions for coordinate inactivity, and finally presenting specific rank calculations and finite-shot comparison results for various quantum settings.
why_interesting: It provides rigorous mathematical tools (Gram matrices, rank analysis) to determine the fundamental limits of parameter estimation in quantum systems, which is crucial for designing robust quantum sensing protocols.
